grammar.title: Gramatyka
grammar.rule: Jest lampa. Nie ma lampy. Jan ma klucz. Jan nie ma klucza. Jan szuka klucza.
grammar.note_en:
The genitive is another noun case: a form showing the noun's job in a sentence. This chapter introduces three uses. Keep them distinct even though the same noun ending often appears in all three.

First, a direct object normally changes from accusative to genitive when its verb is negated. The direct object is what the action is directed at. Jan ma klucz means “Jan has the key”; Jan nie ma klucza means “Jan does not have the key”. Ala ma rysunek / Jan nie ma rysunku means “Ala has the drawing / Jan does not have the drawing”. Jan widzi lampę / Jan nie widzi lampy means “Jan sees the lamp / Jan does not see the lamp”. The word nie stands before the verb. The noun's ending changes because the whole object-taking action is negative. The named subject Jan remains unchanged; this chapter does not teach forms for “I” or “you”.

Second, nie ma can express absence without saying that a person lacks possession. Jest lampa means “There is a lamp”; Nie ma lampy means “There is no lamp”. Jest światło / Nie ma światła means “There is light / There is no light”. In this use ma is part of the absence construction: no person is named as a possessor. Tu jest półka, ale nie ma lampy means “There is a shelf here, but there is no lamp”. Do not replace the absence construction with nie jest: that would not normally mean that the lamp is absent. An object can also be visible in a drawing while the physical object is absent. The story keeps those facts separate.

Third, szukać (“to look for”) takes a genitive noun even in an affirmative sentence. Jan szuka klucza means “Jan is looking for the key”. Jan nie szuka klucza means “Jan is not looking for the key”. Both use klucza. Jan ma klucz / Jan szuka klucza contrasts “Jan has the key / Jan is looking for the key”: search is not a special meaning of possession. Jan szuka lampy means “Jan is looking for the lamp”. Learn the case together with this verb; do not turn every affirmative object into a genitive.

For the feminine nouns shown here, naming -a changes to genitive -y or -i: lampa → lampy (“lamp”), koperta → koperty (“envelope”), kartka → kartki (“note/sheet”), litera → litery (“alphabet letter”). Kartka keeps k and takes -i; do not write kartky. Compare three jobs: kartka is the naming form, kartkę the affirmative object form, and kartki the negative object form. Ewa ma kartkę / Jan nie bierze kartki means “Ewa has a note / Jan does not take the note”. These are singular forms; a familiar-looking final -i does not mean plural here.

The masculine forms must be learned with each noun: klucz → klucza (“key”), ołówek → ołówka (“pencil”), rysunek → rysunku (“drawing”), papier → papieru (“paper”), zamek → zamka (“lock”), przykład → przykładu (“example”), napis → napisu (“inscription”). There is no reliable beginner rule saying every masculine noun takes the same ending. Ołówek loses the e before the final k and retains ó: ołówek → ołówka; rysunek loses the e in rysunku. Zamek loses the e in zamka. Here zamek means a lock, so its genitive is zamka. A different word sense can have a different form; the table does not license every meaning of zamek. The neuter nouns used here change final -o to -a: pudełko → pudełka (“box”) and światło → światła (“light”). Do not infer unshown case forms for the other nouns in this chapter.

Translations for the remaining table phrases are bierze papier / nie bierze papieru (“takes the paper / does not take the paper”), otwiera zamek / nie otwiera zamka (“opens the lock / does not open the lock”), czyta przykład / nie czyta przykładu (“reads the example / does not read the example”), czyta napis / nie czyta napisu (“reads the inscription / does not read the inscription”), and widzi literę / nie widzi litery (“sees the alphabet letter / does not see the alphabet letter”). The tables collect forms already met in this or earlier prose; they are references, not completion exercises.

The inventory note uses the short label Brak, meaning “lack” or “missing”. Ewa immediately explains it with Nie ma lampy (“There is no lamp”). The heading Lampa identifies what the label concerns; the note does not reveal the lamp's location or who took it. Kartka is the flat sheet/note, while koperta is the envelope. Sąsiad and sąsiadka both mean “neighbour”, with male and female reference respectively. Dzień means “day”, wieczór “evening”, and światło “light”; their pictured contrast explains why the missing lamp matters when daylight fades. No past or future tense is introduced.
